title: Homomorphisms
objectives: Prove a map is a homomorphism and find its kernel.

screens.title: Products into sums
screens.prose: A share returns 10% on Monday and loses 10% on Tuesday. Its gross returns $1.10$ and $0.90$ multiply: $1.10 \times 0.90 = 0.99$. Take the natural log of each, as in `exp-log` l6.
screens.question: Fill in each $\ln$ to four decimal places.

hints.text: Use the natural log, the ln key, not log base 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the natural log of each gross return; the last row is $\ln 0.99$.

byKey.r2c2: The last row is $\ln 0.99$. You can also add the two logs above it.

explain.text: The logs add where the returns multiply: $0.09531 + (-0.10536) = -0.01005$. That is $\ln 0.99$. So $\ln$ carries the product of returns to a sum of log returns.

screens.title: Twelve points, three landing places
screens.prose: The points are the 12th roots of unity $\zeta^j$, with $\zeta = e^{2\pi i/12}$ and $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ (`complex` l4). Turns add (`trig` l12), so $z \mapsto z^k$ sends $\zeta^j$ to $\zeta^{kj}$. Move $k$ and watch where the points land.
screens.question: Set $k = 4$. How many of the twelve points land on $1$?

hints.text: Look at the right-hand plane: one image sits at 1 on the real axis.
$\zeta^j$ lands on 1 when $4j$ is a multiple of 12.
$j = 0, 3, 6, 9$ all give $4j \in \{0, 12, 24, 36\}$: four points.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the inputs $j$ with $4j$ a multiple of 12.

byKey.image: You counted the landing places, which are 1, $\zeta^4$ and $\zeta^8$. Count the inputs that land on 1.

explain.text: With $k = 4$, $\zeta^j$ goes to $\zeta^{4j}$. That is 1 exactly when 12 divides $4j$, so for $j = 0, 3, 6, 9$. Four inputs land on each of the three images.

screens.title: Kernel and image
screens.prose: A map $\varphi$ between groups is a **homomorphism** when $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$ for all $a, b$. Here $\varphi(z) = z^4$, and $(zw)^4 = z^4w^4$. The **kernel** $\ker\varphi$ is everything sent to the identity. The **image** $\operatorname{im}\varphi$ is everything it hits.
screens.question: Which $\zeta^j$ are in the kernel of $z \mapsto z^4$? Select all that apply.

options.why: You picked a landing place. $\zeta^4$ is in the image; it goes to $\zeta^{16} = \zeta^4$, not 1.
You took a point two steps round. It goes to $\zeta^8$, not 1.
You picked a landing place. $\zeta^8$ goes to $\zeta^{32} = \zeta^8$, not 1.

hints.text: The identity of the circle group is 1.
$\zeta^j$ is in the kernel when $4j$ is a multiple of 12.
The four you counted on the last screen: $j = 0, 3, 6, 9$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the $\zeta^j$ whose fourth power is 1.

byKey.j4: You chose $\zeta^4$, which is an image point. Its fourth power is $\zeta^{16} = \zeta^4$.

explain.text: The kernel is $\{\zeta^0, \zeta^3, \zeta^6, \zeta^9\}$, four elements. The image is $\{1, \zeta^4, \zeta^8\}$, three elements. Four inputs land on each image point.

screens.title: Which maps keep the structure
screens.prose: Each map must turn the first group's operation into the second's. Check each one against $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$.
screens.question: Which maps are homomorphisms? Select all that apply.

options.why: You took a shift for a homomorphism. It sends 0 to 1, but a homomorphism sends the identity 0 to 0.
You let squaring keep addition. $\varphi(1 + 1) = 4$ but $\varphi(1) + \varphi(1) = 2$.

hints.text: A homomorphism sends the identity to the identity. Test that first.
$\det(\mathbf{AB}) = \det\mathbf{A}\det\mathbf{B}$, and $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma\tau) = \operatorname{sgn}\sigma\operatorname{sgn}\tau$ (l9).
$3(a + b) = 3a + 3b$ holds mod 12. The shift and the square fail.

feedback.correct: Right. Four keep the structure; the shift and the square do not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each map on the identity, then on one pair.

byKey.shift: You kept $x \mapsto x + 1$. It sends 0 to 1, so it cannot be a homomorphism.
byKey.square: You kept squaring. Try $a = b = 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}_8$.

explain.text: The kernels are the matrices with $\det = 1$ (l5), the even permutations $A_n$ (l9), the multiples $n\mathbb{Z}$, and $\{0, 4, 8\}$ for $3x$. The shift moves 0. The square breaks $\varphi(1 + 1) = \varphi(1) + \varphi(1)$.

screens.title: A failing pair
screens.prose: Take $\varphi(x) = x^2 \bmod 8$ on $(\mathbb{Z}_8, +)$. It sends 0 to 0, so the identity test passes. One pair is enough to sink it. Here $\varphi(1) + \varphi(1) = 1 + 1 = 2$.
screens.question: What is $\varphi(1 + 1)$?

hints.text: Work out $1 + 1$ in $\mathbb{Z}_8$ first.
$1 + 1 = 2$, so read the column for $x = 2$.
$\varphi(2) = 4$, which is not 2.

feedback.correct: Right. $\varphi(1 + 1) = 4 \ne 2 = \varphi(1) + \varphi(1)$, so $\varphi$ is not a homomorphism.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the sum $1 + 1 = 2$, then reduce mod 8.

byKey.added: You added $\varphi(1) + \varphi(1)$, which is the other side. Apply $\varphi$ to the sum $2$ instead.

explain.text: $\varphi(2) = 4$ while $\varphi(1) + \varphi(1) = 2$. The two sides differ, so squaring does not keep addition. Passing the identity test is necessary, not sufficient.

screens.title: Identity and inverses
screens.prose: Every homomorphism $\varphi : G \to H$ sends $e_G$ to $e_H$ and inverses to inverses. A linear map does the same with $T(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{0}$ (`linear-maps` l5). One line below is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.why: You assumed the first fact. A function may send $e_G$ anywhere; the homomorphism rule forces $e_H$.

hints.text: Start from $e_G = e_G e_G$.
Cancel one $\varphi(e_G)$ from $\varphi(e_G) = \varphi(e_G)\varphi(e_G)$.
Then show $\varphi(a)\varphi(a^{-1}) = e_H$ and use unique inverses.

feedback.correct: Right. The identity first, then inverses from it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Prove $\varphi(e_G) = e_H$ first, then use it for inverses.

byKey.d1: You used a line that assumes the result. Being a function says nothing about where $e_G$ goes.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: $\varphi(e_G)$ equals its own square, and cancelling gives $e_H$. Then $\varphi(a)\varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(e_G) = e_H$. Inverses are unique, so $\varphi(a^{-1}) = \varphi(a)^{-1}$.

screens.title: The kernel is a subgroup
screens.prose: The one-step test of l5: a non-empty subset $S$ with $ab^{-1} \in S$ for all $a, b \in S$ is a subgroup. Apply it to $\ker\varphi$. One line below is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: $\varphi(e) = e$, so $e \in \ker\varphi$ and the kernel is not empty (last screen).
Let $a, b \in \ker\varphi$, so $\varphi(a) = \varphi(b) = e$ (definition of kernel).
So $\ker\varphi$ is a subgroup of $G$ (one-step test, l5).
$\varphi(ab) = e$, so $ab \in \ker\varphi$, which is all we need (closure).
lines.why: You checked products only. The one-step test asks for $ab^{-1}$, which also covers inverses.

hints.text: Show the kernel is not empty first.
Then take two kernel elements and compute $\varphi(ab^{-1})$.
Order: non-empty, take $a, b$, compute, conclude by the one-step test.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The test needs a non-empty set and $ab^{-1}$ inside it.

byKey.d1: You used closure under products. That misses inverses; the test needs $ab^{-1}$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: The kernel holds $e$, so it is not empty. For $a, b$ in it, $\varphi(ab^{-1}) = e\,e^{-1} = e$. The one-step test then makes it a subgroup.

screens.title: Is it even a function
screens.prose: Try $\varphi : \mathbb{Z}_6 \to \mathbb{Z}_4$, $\varphi(x) = x \bmod 4$. In $\mathbb{Z}_6$ the integers 0 and 6 name the same element, and so do 1 and 7.
screens.question: Is $\varphi$ a homomorphism?

options.text: No. It is not even a function: the element $0$ would go to both 0 and 2.
Yes. Reduction modulo a number is a homomorphism.
options.why: You trusted the formula. It works from $\mathbb{Z}$, and from $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ since 4 divides 12, but 4 does not divide 6.

options.text: Yes. $\varphi(a + b) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(b)$ for $a, b$ from 0 to 5.
options.why: You checked one name of each element. In $\mathbb{Z}_6$, $3 + 3 = 0$, yet $\varphi(3) + \varphi(3) = 2$ in $\mathbb{Z}_4$.
You tested the identity, and $0 \bmod 4 = 0$ passes. The trouble is that 0 also has the name 6.

hints.text: Feed the map two names of the same element.
0 and 6 are the same element of $\mathbb{Z}_6$.
$0 \bmod 4 = 0$ but $6 \bmod 4 = 2$, so one element gets two outputs.

feedback.correct: Right. A rule on names must agree on every name of an element.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the outputs for 0 and 6, which are one element of $\mathbb{Z}_6$.

byKey.always: You trusted the formula $x \bmod 4$. It is well defined from $\mathbb{Z}_n$ only when 4 divides $n$.

explain.text: The element 0 of $\mathbb{Z}_6$ has names 0 and 6, and the rule gives 0 and 2. So the rule does not define a function. From $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ it works, since adding 12 adds a multiple of 4.

screens.title: Injective exactly when the kernel is trivial
screens.prose: A map is injective when different inputs give different outputs (`proof` l9). A linear map is injective exactly when its kernel is zero (`linear-maps` l6). Groups pass the same test. If $\varphi$ is injective, only $e$ goes to $e$; prove the converse.
screens.question: Prove: if $\ker\varphi = \{e\}$, then $\varphi$ is injective. Leave out the flawed line.

lines.text: Then $\varphi(a)^{-1}\varphi(b) = e$ (multiply on the left by $\varphi(a)^{-1}$).
So $a^{-1}b = e$, and $a = b$ (multiply on the left by $a$).
$\varphi(a) = \varphi(b)$, so $a = b$ since $\varphi$ is a homomorphism.
lines.why: That line assumes injectivity, which we are proving. A homomorphism alone need not be one to one.

hints.text: Move everything to one side: look at $a^{-1}b$.
$\varphi(a^{-1}b) = \varphi(a)^{-1}\varphi(b) = e$.
So $a^{-1}b$ is in the kernel, which is only $e$.

feedback.correct: Right. Equal images put $a^{-1}b$ in the kernel.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn $\varphi(a) = \varphi(b)$ into a statement about $a^{-1}b$.

byKey.d1: You concluded $a = b$ straight away. That is injectivity itself, the thing to prove.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: Equal images give $\varphi(a^{-1}b) = e$. So $a^{-1}b$ lies in the kernel, which is $\{e\}$. Hence $a = b$.

screens.title: A check digit
screens.prose: A SEDOL is a London security code: six characters and a check digit. For a numeric stem, the check digit makes the weighted sum, with weights $1, 3, 1, 7, 3, 9, 1$, equal $0 \bmod 10$. The stem here is 026349.
screens.question: What check digit completes 026349?

hints.text: Add the six products first.
The check digit has weight 1 and must lift 126 to a multiple of 10.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the digit that brings 126 up to a multiple of 10.

byKey.remainder: You took $126 \bmod 10 = 6$. The check digit must bring the sum to a multiple of 10, so it is $10 - 6$.

explain.text: The six products sum to 126. Adding $4 \times 1$ gives 130, which is $0 \bmod 10$. So the full code is 0263494.

screens.title: Errors the check misses
screens.prose: The weighted sum is a homomorphism from $\mathbb{Z}_{10}^7$ to $\mathbb{Z}_{10}$, and the valid codes are its kernel. Changing one digit by $d$ changes the sum by $wd$. Every weight is a unit mod 10, so every single-digit error is caught. Swapping neighbours $a, b$ changes the sum by $(w_1 - w_2)(a - b)$.
screens.question: Which swaps of two neighbouring digits slip through?

options.text: Swaps of two digits that differ by 5, since every weight difference is even.
None, because each weight is a unit.
options.why: You carried the single-digit result over. A swap multiplies $a - b$ by $w_1 - w_2$, and that difference is even, not a unit.

options.text: Every swap, since the same digits are still there.
options.why: You assumed the sum ignores order. The weights differ, so most swaps change the sum.

options.text: Only swaps of two equal digits.
options.why: Swapping equal digits is no error at all. Digits 5 apart also slip, since $2 \times 5 = 10$.

hints.text: Every weight difference in the table is even.
An even number times $a - b$ is $0 \bmod 10$ when $a - b$ is a multiple of 5.
So digits 5 apart, such as 1 and 6, swap unseen.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask when $(w_1 - w_2)(a - b)$ is a multiple of 10.

byKey.none: You used the single-digit argument. A swap's change is a weight difference times $a - b$, and the differences are even.

explain.text: Each weight difference is even, so $a - b = \pm 5$ makes the change a multiple of 10. Stems starting 16 and 61 give $1 + 18 = 19$ and $6 + 3 = 9$, which agree mod 10. So they get the same check digit.

screens.title: Test every pair
screens.prose: A map $\mathbb{Z}_n \to \mathbb{Z}_m$ is a list `f` of length $n$. Write `is_hom(f, n, m)`, checking $f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b)$ for every pair, and `kernel(f)`. Checking every pair proves the property for that one finite group only.

params.title: Expected
lines: >>> f = [3 * x % 12 for x in range(12)]

screens.question: Complete both functions.

examples.call: is_hom([3 * x % 12 for x in range(12)], 12, 12)
kernel([3 * x % 12 for x in range(12)])

tests.call: is_hom([3 * x % 12 for x in range(12)], 12, 12)
kernel([3 * x % 12 for x in range(12)])
is_hom([x * x % 8 for x in range(8)], 8, 8)
is_hom([2 * x % 6 for x in range(3)], 3, 6)

widget.how: The first Check starts Python, which takes a few seconds. Submit runs 10 hidden tests; each must equal the expected value exactly.

hints.text: Loop over every $a$ and $b$ in range(n).
Compare `f[(a + b) % n]` with `(f[a] + f[b]) % m`.
For the kernel, keep each x whose f[x] is 0.

feedback.correct: Right. Every pair passes for $3x$; squaring fails at $a = b = 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test every pair, reducing the sum mod n on the left and mod m on the right.

explain.text: `is_hom` tries all $n^2$ pairs, which settles the question for that finite group. The kernel of $3x$ on $\mathbb{Z}_{12}$ is $[0, 4, 8]$. The list for $x \bmod 4$ on $\mathbb{Z}_6$ fails at $3 + 3$.

ideas: A homomorphism keeps the operation: $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$. It then sends $e$ to $e$ and inverses to inverses.
The kernel, everything sent to $e$, is a subgroup. A homomorphism is injective exactly when its kernel is $\{e\}$.
A rule on residues must give one output per element. $x \bmod 4$ is well defined from $\mathbb{Z}_n$ only when 4 divides $n$.
summary.trap: Checking a formula on one name per residue. $0$ and $6$ are one element of $\mathbb{Z}_6$, yet differ mod 4.

quiz.prose: A SEDOL uses weights 1, 3, 1, 7, 3, 9, 1 modulo 10. Every single-digit typing error is caught.
quiz.question: Why?

options.text: Each weight is a unit mod 10, so $wd \not\equiv 0$ for $d \not\equiv 0$.

options.why: You trusted odd weights. Odd is not enough: a weight 5 would miss $d = 2$, since $5 \times 2 = 10$.
You looked for distinct weights, but two positions share weight 1 and two share 3. Each weight on its own matters.
You looked at position. A unit weight catches the change wherever the digit sits.

feedback.correct: Right. Multiplying by a unit is injective.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask when $wd$ can be $0 \bmod 10$.

explain.text: A change $d$ in a digit of weight $w$ changes the sum by $wd$. Multiplying by a unit mod 10 sends only 0 to 0. So $wd \not\equiv 0$ and the error shows.

quiz.prose: The trivial map $\varphi : G \to H$ sends every $g$ to $e_H$.
quiz.question: What is $\ker\varphi$?

options.why: You recalled the injective case. Here every element goes to the identity, so every element is in the kernel.
A kernel always holds $e_G$, since $\varphi(e_G) = e_H$.
You picked the target group. The kernel lives in $G$, the domain.

feedback.correct: Right. Everything goes to the identity.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The kernel is everything that goes to the identity.

explain.text: Every $g$ goes to $e_H$, so every $g$ is in the kernel. The kernel is all of $G$. The image is $\{e_H\}$.

quiz.prose: An **isomorphism** is a bijective homomorphism. Consider $\ln : (\mathbb{R}_{>0}, \times) \to (\mathbb{R}, +)$.
quiz.question: Is $\ln$ an isomorphism?

options.text: Yes. $\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b$, and $\ln$ is a bijection with inverse $e^x$.
No, $\ln$ of a negative number is undefined.
options.why: You looked outside the domain. The domain is the positive reals, where $\ln$ is defined.

options.text: No, it turns products into sums, so the operations differ.
options.why: You expected one operation on both sides. An isomorphism may match one operation to another.

options.text: No, it misses the negative reals.
options.why: You thought the image stops at 0. $\ln x$ is negative for $0 < x < 1$, so every real is hit.

feedback.correct: Right. Log returns and gross returns carry the same structure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the homomorphism rule, then whether $\ln$ is one to one and onto.

explain.text: $\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b$, so $\ln$ is a homomorphism. It has inverse $e^x$, so it is a bijection. So $(\mathbb{R}_{>0}, \times) \cong (\mathbb{R}, +)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the $x$ with $4x$ a multiple of 12.

byKey.image: You counted the image $\{0, 4, 8\}$. The kernel is the set of inputs that go to 0.

explain.text: $4x \equiv 0 \pmod{12}$ exactly when 3 divides $x$. So the kernel is $\{0, 3, 6, 9\}$, with 4 elements. The image $\{0, 4, 8\}$ has 3.
